newsitem.title: UK: Unrealistic to revoke existing arms licences -UK.
newsitem.headline: Unrealistic to revoke existing arms licences -UK.

text.p: Britain's Labour government said on Monday it would not revoke arms export licences approved by the previous Conservative administration.

The announcement, made by Foreign Secretary Robin Cook in a written parliamentary answer, would appear to give a green light to British Aerospace Plc to proceed with the previously agreed export of 16 Hawk fighters to Indonesia.

Cook was unveiling the criteria the government will apply to implement its election manifesto commitment to ban weapons exports to regimes that might use them for internal repression or international aggression.
Cook mentioned no countries or types of weapons that might be affected by the new guidelines.
"They are universal criteria. They are not aimed at any one country in particular, but they will apply even-handedly to all countries," Cook said.

An official later confirmed that BAe's export of 16 Hawks would go ahead by virtue of the fact that ministers had concluded that all existing arms licences -- totalling more than 21,000 -- must be honoured.
"There is no blacklist," he said.
Officials said the guidelines announced by Cook hardened the Labour government's position on arms exports in two respects.

Firstly, in deciding whether to licence weapons sales, officials will have to consider whether there is clear evidence of the recent use of "similar equipment" for internal repression by the end-user. Equipment supplied by other arms exports will thus come under scrutiny.

Secondly, the threshold for banning exports has been lowered. Whereas Labour spoke previously of weapons that were "likely" to be used for internal repression, Cook said the ban would apply if the arms "might" be used for repressive purposes.

In a related parliamentary amswer, Cook said the government was fulfilling its manifesto commitment to ban the export in any circumstances of electro-shock batons, stun guns, leg-irons or similar instruments of inhuman or degrading treatment.
In the interest of transparency, the government will issue an annual report on the application of its export controls.
Cook said the nature of the equipment proposed for export would have to be carefully considered.
"Certain goods have more obvious potential for use in internal repression than others, such as armoured personnel carriers specially designed for internal security," he said.
The criteria will not be applied mechanistically, and judgement will always be required, Cook said.
For example, the use of force by a government within its own borders does not always constitute internal repression, he said.
Using force to preserve law and order against terrorists or other criminals is legitimate as long as it is in accordance with international human rights standards, Cook added.
He said the government would not issue an export licence if there is a clearly identifiable risk that the intended recipient would use the arms aggressively against another country.
"However, a purely theoretical possibility that the items concerned might be used in the future against another state will not of itself lead to a licence being refused," he said.
Labour was not responsible for the export licences issued by the Conservatives, who were ousted at the May 1 election after 18 years in power.
"We do not, however, consider it would be realistic or practical to revoke licences which were valid and in force at the time of our election," Cook said.
